ratings.plot: A young man and woman meet on a train in Europe, and wind up spending one evening together in Vienna. Unfortunately, both know that this will probably be their only night together.

verdict.reason: One of Linklater's essential films — a master class in dialogue and intimacy that demands the theater's full attention. Metrograph's restoration gives you the Vienna streets and faces in the clarity they deserve.

ratings.plot: A young woman returns to her hometown of Turin to set up a new fashion salon and gets involved with a troubled woman and her three wealthy friends.

verdict.reason: Antonioni's debut feature is essential cinema about desire and class in postwar Italy, and this restoration at Metrograph makes the austere compositions sing on the big screen. The film's cool formalism masks genuine emotional wreckage—watch it for the way he frames loneliness as a spatial problem, not a feeling.

ratings.plot: A truck driver stops at a small family-run noodle shop and decides to help its fledgling business. The story is intertwined with various vignettes about the relationship of love and food.

verdict.reason: One of the funniest films about food and desire ever made—see it on a big screen where the anarchic energy and visual gags land hard. Itami's digressive structure and absurdist humor demand theatrical immediacy, and this DCP restoration at Metrograph gives the film's saturated colors and precise compositions the space they need.

movies.title: Days and Nights in the Forest

verdict.reason: Essential Ray on the big screen — this ranks among his finest character studies. The Metrograph restoration reveals the subtle interplay between natural light and psychological insight that makes his camera work irreplaceable.

movies.title: Four Adventures of Reinette and Mirabelle

ratings.plot: Two unlike girls are going to learn each other's world - lovely countryside and bustling Paris.

verdict.reason: A Rohmer film about friendship and class collision belongs on the big screen, and this Metrograph restoration captures the precise social observation that makes his work essential. The four-part structure lets each encounter breathe—the kind of patient filmmaking that demands theatrical attention.

ratings.plot: The Tramp cares for an abandoned child, but events put their relationship in jeopardy.

verdict.reason: One of cinema's essential films and a rare chance to see Chaplin's masterpiece on the big screen where its visual storytelling demands to be experienced. The final sequence—a dream of redemption that transforms despair into grace—only works in a theater.

movies.title: How to Divorce During the War

ratings.plot: Set in Vilnius in 2022, high-flying executive Marija chooses the worst moment to discuss divorce with husband Vytas - one day before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The couple navigates separation amid a refugee crisis.

verdict.reason: A debut feature that finds emotional clarity in catastrophic timing, using a single marriage to frame the chaos of invasion. Blazevicius shoots Vilnius with the precision of a architect documenting a city about to break.

movies.title: Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma

ratings.plot: A queer director making a slasher franchise sequel becomes obsessed with casting the original film's 'final girl,' leading both women into psychological and sexual chaos.

verdict.reason: Schoenbrun's follow-up to We're All Going to the World's Fair is sharp, weird, and genuinely funny in ways that justify the hype. The 35mm print at Angelika gives the film's garish colors and grotesque set pieces the theatrical punch they demand.

ratings.plot: The parallel coming-of-age stories of a father living in Sarajevo during World War II and his son living through the Siege of Sarajevo during the Bosnian War.

verdict.reason: A rare Bosnian film about generational trauma across two wars deserves to be seen on a big screen. Film Forum's programming of this restoration makes it a necessary theatrical moment for a film that has circulated too little outside festival circuits.

ratings.plot: Documentary filmmaker Ross McElwee sets out to make a movie about Union General Sherman's March to the Sea towards the end of the American Civil War, but keeps getting sidetracked by his own love life.

verdict.reason: One of the great American experimental documentaries deserves to be seen theatrically in its full rambling glory. Ross McElwee's four-hour digression from General Sherman to his own romantic misadventures is a singular work of cinema that only works as a committed sit-down experience.

ratings.plot: Eight-year-old Ahmed has mistakenly taken his friend Mohammad's notebook. He wants to return it, or else his friend will be expelled from school. The boy determinedly sets out to find Mohammad's home in the neighbouring village.

verdict.reason: Kiarostami's breakthrough transforms a simple premise into profound cinema. The Iranian landscape and natural light create images that lose impact on small screens.

ratings.plot: A mysterious woman persuades two cowboys to help her in a revenge scheme.

verdict.reason: A restored 35mm print of Monte Hellman's desert masterpiece is a rare gift—this is the way to see one of the great American Westerns. The sparse dialogue and mythic framing create a vision of the West that still has no peer, and Anthology's presentation honors every deliberate frame.

ratings.plot: A troubled child summons the courage to help a friendly alien escape from Earth and return to his home planet.

verdict.reason: Essential big screen viewing for one of Spielberg's most emotionally direct films. John Williams' soaring theme and the bicycle chase finale demand theatrical sound and scale.

ratings.plot: Pulp novelist Holly Martins travels to shadowy, postwar Vienna, only to find himself investigating the mysterious death of an old friend, Harry Lime.

verdict.reason: This is essential cinema—see it on the biggest screen available. Carol Reed's use of Dutch angles and Vienna's bomb-crater geography makes this a film that demands theatrical space.

ratings.plot: Paddington, now happily settled with the Brown family and a popular member of the local community, picks up a series of odd jobs to buy the perfect present for his Aunt Lucy's 100th birthday, only for the gift to be stolen.

verdict.reason: A family film with the visual precision and emotional intelligence of a great animated feature, executed in live action. Paul King's framing, blocking, and color sense elevate every frame beyond what the premise demands.

ratings.plot: Set in early 19th century Romania, a policeman, Costandin, is hired by a nobleman to find a Gypsy slave who has run away from his estate after having an affair with his wife.

verdict.reason: A masterwork of moral clarity disguised as a picaresque road movie—Radu Jude's command of image and dialogue is absolute. Metrograph is showing it in DCP, which preserves the film's stark black-and-white composition and the precision of every frame.

ratings.plot: A self-conscious woman juggles adjusting to her new role as an aristocrat's wife and avoiding being intimidated by his first wife's spectral presence.

verdict.reason: Hitchcock's only Best Picture winner holds up as a masterclass in psychological suspense and Gothic atmosphere on the big screen. Metrograph's DCP restoration brings out the shadows and compositions that make this 1940 film feel as immediate as a modern thriller.

movies.title: Marcel the Shell with Shoes On

ratings.plot: A cash-strapped documentary maker decides to make his newest documentary about a mollusk shell he finds living in his Airbnb with his friends.

verdict.reason: A genuinely original film that earns its emotional weight through tiny, precise details and a real voice—see it before word-of-mouth turns it into a meme. Fleischer-Camp's stop-motion work captures something between live-action documentary and animation that feels like nothing else in theaters.

ratings.plot: A 19-year-old Anthony Bourdain travels to Provincetown and stumbles into the chaotic world of a restaurant kitchen, setting off a summer that will shape the course of his life.

verdict.reason: Matt Johnson turns Bourdain's formative summer into a film about ambition, kitchen chaos, and sexual awakening that moves with real energy. The performances crackle and the period detail feels lived-in rather than studied.

ratings.plot: A family of six settles into their new home on Vancouver Island as internal dynamics are slowly revealed through the eyes of the youngest child.

verdict.reason: See this intimate family portrait while it has theatrical momentum. Romvari shoots through a child's perspective with uncommon sensitivity to how kids actually process adult tensions.

ratings.plot: A counterfeit bill that starts off as a schoolboy prank leads to incarceration and violence.

verdict.reason: Bresson's final film is a masterpiece of moral devastation that demands the theater. The DCP restoration at Metrograph shows the crystalline austerity of his compositions and the accumulating weight of casual cruelty with devastating clarity.

ratings.plot: After a bad gambling bet, a schoolteacher is marooned in a town full of crazy, drunk, violent men who threaten to make him just as crazy, drunk, and violent.

verdict.reason: One of the great films about masculine violence and social collapse—see it on the big screen while you can. Metrograph is showing a restored DCP of a 1971 masterpiece that demands theater sound and image to land its full nightmare force.

ratings.plot: Nelly has just lost her grandmother and is helping her parents clean out her mother's childhood home. She explores the house and the surrounding woods. One day she meets a girl her age building a tree-house.

verdict.reason: Sciamma's shortest film is also her most direct statement about time, memory, and the people we become—see it on the big screen while you can. At 73 minutes, it respects your night and leaves you changed.

movies.title: Mary Oliver: Saved by the Beauty of the World

verdict.reason: Skip the streaming queue and catch this at IFC Center while it plays—a rare theatrical chance to sit with Oliver's voice in a room full of people who need it. The film moves through her life with the same attention to detail she brought to watching the world, letting silence do half the work.

ratings.plot: Joe and Angela's marriage is on thin ice. When they invite their enigmatic upstairs neighbors for a dinner party, the night spirals into unexpected places.

verdict.reason: Olivia Wilde directs a sharp ensemble comedy about marriage and desire that earns its runtime with wit and genuine stakes. The dinner-party setup becomes a pressure cooker for real friction, not just plot mechanics.

ratings.plot: Kateri loses her mother, leaves foster care. Reunites with former foster parent Amziah who mentors her, revealing hidden skills. Faces devastating situation, relies on newfound strength to seek justice.

verdict.reason: Andrew Patterson has made a gripping crime thriller with real narrative momentum and sharp direction. The 130-minute runtime feels earned, building toward a climax that justifies the patient setup.

ratings.plot: The life of Mason, from early childhood to his arrival at college.

verdict.reason: Linklater's twelve-year experiment in time-lapse cinema remains a singular achievement in form and patience. The 165-minute runtime is the point, not a liability—you're watching actual years compress into an evening.

ratings.plot: On lakeside summer holiday, a conflicted older man is dared to have a flirt with two beautiful teenage half-sisters despite his betrothal to a diplomat's daughter and the fact that the girls have boyfriends.

verdict.reason: Rohmer's masterpiece of desire and moral restraint deserves the big screen. Metrograph's DCP restoration brings out the precision of his compositions and the lake light that makes every conversation feel like it matters.

ratings.plot: This Hong Kong-set crime drama follows the lives of a hitman, hoping to get out of the business, and his elusive female partner.

verdict.reason: Wong Kar-Wai at peak visual invention deserves the big screen, and this neon-soaked crime film moves with a kinetic energy that streaming kills. Metrograph's DCP presentation restores the chromatic intensity that makes every frame feel like a deliberate painting.

ratings.plot: A girl with few real prospects joins a gang, reinventing herself and gaining a sense of self confidence in the process. However, she soon finds that this new life does not necessarily make her any happier.

verdict.reason: Sciamma captures the texture of female adolescence with visual precision and restraint that most coming-of-age films never achieve. The 4:3 aspect ratio and handheld intimacy at Metrograph demand the theatrical frame.

ratings.plot: 24 hours in the lives of three young men in the French suburbs the day after a violent riot.

verdict.reason: One of the essential films about urban rage and class in cinema, and Metrograph's DCP restoration makes this the right place to see it. Kassovitz's black-and-white cinematography and the unflinching 98-minute sprint through a single day demand the big screen.

ratings.plot: A devout Catholic man's rigid principles are challenged during a one-night stay with Maud, a divorced woman with an outsize personality.

verdict.reason: One of Rohmer's essential moral comedies, built on sharp dialogue and the collision between dogma and desire. Metrograph's DCP restoration makes the Parisian interiors and winter light sing in ways the home version cannot match.

ratings.plot: Based on Honobu Yonezawa's novel. Set in 16th century Japan, follows Lord Murashige Araki who, besieged in his castle, confronts mysterious crimes and allies with imprisoned strategist Kanbei Kuroda to uncover the truth.

verdict.reason: Kurosawa's first English-language film is a taut mystery that moves like a thriller despite its historical setting, with the kind of visual clarity his best work demands. Catch it at BAM or Film Forum for the full restoration.

ratings.plot: A war-hardened general, egged on by his ambitious wife, works to fulfill a prophecy that he would become lord of Spider's Web Castle.

verdict.reason: One of the essential Shakespeare adaptations on film—Kurosawa's reimagining of Macbeth as a samurai tragedy is a masterpiece of visual storytelling that demands the big screen. The fog-shrouded castle, the arrow-death finale, and Isuzu Yamada's performance create a work that stands entirely on its own, not in the shadow of the play.

ratings.plot: Odysseus, king of Ithaca, embarks on a perilous journey to return home after the Trojan War.

verdict.reason: Nolan's epic delivers exactly what you want from 172 minutes and a $250 million budget: scale, spectacle, and a story that earns its runtime. See it in 70mm or IMAX at Lincoln Square if you can.

ratings.plot: After his family is murdered by a notorious and ruthless bandit, a former police officer enlists the services of two outlaws to capture the bandit.

verdict.reason: One of cinema's great action films—see it restored on a big screen at Metrograph. The DCP brings new life to Ramesh Sippy's 1975 masterpiece of wit, violence, and friendship that shaped Hindi cinema for decades.

ratings.plot: While a zombie virus breaks out in South Korea, passengers struggle to survive on the train from Seoul to Busan.

verdict.reason: A restrained zombie film that uses genre mechanics to examine human selfishness under pressure—rare enough to justify the trip. The restoration at IFC Center sharpens the kinetic train-set staging that made this work in the first place.

ratings.plot: A documentary about writer and director Brian De Palma.

verdict.reason: Essential viewing for anyone serious about cinema craft and narrative design. Baumbach and Paltrow let De Palma himself do the teaching, breaking down how he builds suspense and composes a frame with the precision of a surgeon.

ratings.plot: Two boys begin a silence strike to press their parents into buying them a television set.

verdict.reason: One of Ozu's masterpieces about Japanese family life, rendered in color for the first time in this restoration. The deadpan humor and formal compositions make this a rare theatrical event that demands a big screen.

ratings.plot: When her grandson is kidnapped during the Tour de France, Madame Souza and her beloved pooch Bruno team up with the Belleville Sisters--an aged song-and-dance team from the days of Fred Astaire--to rescue him.

verdict.reason: One of the great hand-drawn comedies—a film that moves, sings, and surprises without a single line of dialogue for the first twenty minutes. Metrograph's DCP screening honors Chomet's intricate frame-by-frame animation work, where every background gag and sight line matters.

ratings.plot: A former San Francisco police detective juggles wrestling with his personal demons and becoming obsessed with the hauntingly beautiful woman he has been hired to trail, who may be deeply disturbed.

verdict.reason: One of cinema's greatest achievements belongs on the big screen, and this 35mm print at Metrograph is the way to experience Hitchcock's command of color, space, and visual obsession. The vertigo effect and San Francisco locations demand theatrical scale to hit their full hypnotic power.

ratings.plot: When a menace known as the Joker wreaks havoc and chaos on the people of Gotham, Batman, James Gordon and Harvey Dent must work together to put an end to the madness.

verdict.reason: Watch it. Metrograph is showing the 35mm print, which is the only way to see Nolan's compositions as intended.

ratings.plot: After a threat from the tiger Shere Khan forces him to flee the jungle, a man-cub named Mowgli embarks on a journey of self discovery with the help of panther Bagheera and free-spirited bear Baloo.

verdict.reason: Favreau's photorealistic animation remains a technical marvel that demands the theatrical image. Metrograph's 35mm print is the ideal way to see the jungle rendered at this scale and clarity.

movies.title: There Once Was a Singing Blackbird

ratings.plot: A carefree young percussionist roams the streets of Tbilisi, interacting with friends and strangers alike, and tries to avoid responsibilities.

verdict.reason: A rare chance to see Iosseliani's debut in a restored DCP at Metrograph. The film's gentle comedy and kinetic street-level observation of Tbilisi justify the trip for anyone interested in Soviet-era cinema outside the monumental tradition.

movies.title: Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown

ratings.plot: A television actress encounters a variety of eccentric characters after embarking on a journey to discover why her lover abruptly left her.

verdict.reason: Essential Almodóvar at peak invention, vital in 35mm. The 88-minute runtime moves like a perfectly wound toy, and Metrograph's print restores the saturated color palette that makes every frame feel like a poster.

ratings.plot: Henry Graham lives the life of a playboy. When his lawyer tells him that his lifestyle has consumed all his funds, Henry must avoid climbing down the social ladder. He plans to marry wealthy scientist Henrietta Lowell - and kill her.

verdict.reason: Worth seeing for May's brilliant directorial debut, which she also wrote and starred in with perfect misanthropic timing. Her chemistry with Walter Matthau creates one of the sharpest dark comedies of the 1970s.

ratings.plot: Carrie White, a shy, friendless teenage girl who is sheltered by her domineering, religious mother, unleashes her telekinetic powers after being humiliated by her classmates at her senior prom.

verdict.reason: De Palma's horror masterpiece belongs on the big screen, where the split-screen prom sequence and Sissy Spacek's performance hit hardest. The Alamo locations will pack it with the right crowd.

ratings.plot: In Detroit, a pop-culture enthusiast steals cocaine from his new wife's pimp and tries to sell it in Hollywood, prompting the mobsters who own the drugs to pursue the couple.

verdict.reason: Tony Scott's greatest film—a pulp romance that moves with genuine velocity and heartbreak. The Metrograph screening gives you the color saturation and kinetic editing that define Scott's visual language.

ratings.plot: A comedy (sort of) about young men in America.

verdict.reason: Oscar Boyson's debut is a sharp, confident comedy that earns its genre ambitions in 91 unpadded minutes. The film moves with real wit and finds fresh angles on American masculinity without collapsing into familiar beats.

ratings.plot: Alice, an ambitious camgirl, wakes up one day to discover she's been replaced on her show with an exact replica of herself.

verdict.reason: A smart horror film about identity and digital labor that uses its premise to say something true about performance and violation. Goldhaber sustains the tension through tight 94 minutes and finds real dread in the uncanny—the double isn't a jump-scare trick but a slowly darkening mirror.

ratings.plot: Mysterious boat returns to a village 30 years after vanishing. Two men join its crew hoping for better fortune. After one voyage, they find themselves transported back in time, mistaken for the original crew.

verdict.reason: Mark Jenkin's time-slip fantasy demands the big screen and his control of mood is worth experiencing in a theater. Lincoln Center is showing a filmmaker working at the height of his powers in a film built on texture, strangeness, and the uncanny.

ratings.plot: Two 12-year-olds, who live on an island, fall in love with each other and elope into the wilderness. While people set out on a search mission, a violent storm approaching them catches their attention.

verdict.reason: Anderson's most purely joyful film deserves the big screen, and 94 minutes means no endurance test. The composition, color, and symmetry reward theatrical projection in ways streaming cannot touch.

ratings.plot: When greedy tycoons refuse to return Mothra's egg to the people of Infant Island, they must decide if they are willing to answer Japan's own pleas for help when Godzilla arises near Nagoya.

verdict.reason: This is peak Toho kaiju craft from Honda at his most confident, balancing spectacle with genuine visual wit. The miniature work and suit choreography in the final battle remain thrilling on a big screen, and the film's satirical edge about corporate greed bites harder than most monster movies ever dare.

ratings.plot: Two neighbors form a strong bond after both suspect extramarital activities of their spouses. However, they agree to keep their bond platonic so as not to commit similar wrongs.

verdict.reason: Wong Kar-Wai's masterpiece deserves the big screen, and Metrograph's 35mm print restores the chromatic precision that defines his visual language. The film's emotional restraint and compositional density reveal themselves only in a theater.

ratings.plot: A young woman, studying to be a vet, develops a craving for human flesh.

verdict.reason: Ducournau's debut is a rare horror film that earns its extremity through formal precision and genuine artistic vision. Metrograph's DCP presentation showcases the film's composed cinematography and color work, which are essential to how the body horror lands.

ratings.plot: A psychologist is sent to a station orbiting a distant planet in order to discover what has caused the crew to go insane.

verdict.reason: Worth the trip for one of cinema's greatest meditations on memory and identity, shot with Tarkovsky's hypnotic command of space and time. Metrograph's DCP restoration honors the film's deliberate pacing and architectural cinematography on a proper screen.

ratings.plot: Anna, a shy 12-year-old girl, is sent to spend time with her aunt and uncle who live in the countryside, where she meets Marnie. The two become best friends. But Anna gradually discovers that Marnie is not quite who she appears to...

verdict.reason: Studio Ghibli's final feature is a delicate ghost story about loneliness and connection that demands the big screen. Yonebayashi's watercolor animation and the Metrograph's DCP projection bring out textures that would dissolve on a small display.

ratings.plot: A filmmaking family finds themselves in a real-life horror movie when a body turns up on the set of their low-budget slasher, forcing them to cover up the murder to keep filming.

verdict.reason: Skip the streaming wait and catch this high-concept comedy-horror on the big screen where the tonal shifts land hardest. The 81-minute runtime means no fat, and that premise needs the sudden violence of theatrical sound to work.

ratings.plot: A group of shoplifters take aim at a cutthroat fashion maven by stealing her clothes and reselling them at a lower price, what they call "fashion-forward philanthropy."

verdict.reason: Riley delivers his sharpest social satire yet with perfect tonal control. The fashion industry backdrop gives him fresh material to skewer capitalism with his signature wit.

ratings.plot: After a botched bank robbery lands his younger brother in prison, Connie Nikas embarks on a twisted odyssey through New York City's underworld to get his brother Nick out of jail.

verdict.reason: Watch it. The Safdies pack 102 minutes with kinetic tension and Adam Sandler doing raw, desperate work, and Metrograph's 35mm print restores the nocturnal neon palette that makes this film move.

ratings.plot: The discovery of a severed human ear found in a field leads a young man on an investigation related to a beautiful, mysterious nightclub singer and a group of psychopathic criminals who have kidnapped her child.

verdict.reason: Lynch's masterpiece of American noir perversion demands the big screen and the dark theater it requires. The sound design alone—those industrial drones, that pop song, Penderecki's strings—creates an atmosphere no home setup can match.

ratings.plot: A humble clerk courts a woman who awaits her lover's return night after night.

verdict.reason: Visconti's 1957 masterwork on desire and self-deception belongs on the big screen, and Film Forum's restoration makes this the time to see it. The nocturnal Rome cinematography and Marcello Mastroianni's performance justify the trip.

ratings.plot: A nerdy florist finds his chance for success and romance with the help of a giant man-eating plant who demands to be fed.

verdict.reason: Go to Alamo Drafthouse; Frank Oz's musical comedy belongs in a theater where the fun can breathe. The songs and Rick Moranis's nervy charm demand a crowd.

movies.title: We're All Going to the World's Fair

ratings.plot: Alone in her attic bedroom, teenager Casey becomes immersed in an online role-playing horror game, wherein she begins to document the changes that may or may not be happening to her.

verdict.reason: Schoenbrun's debut captures the disorienting blur between online ritual and genuine psychological unraveling with unnerving precision. The found-footage aesthetic and real-time screen recordings make the dread feel immediate and tactile in ways streaming cannot replicate.

movies.title: What Ever Happened to Baby Jane? (1962)

ratings.plot: A former vaudeville child star torments her paraplegic sister, who eclipsed her as a movie star, in their decaying Hollywood mansion while desperately clinging to hopes of a comeback.

verdict.reason: Essential viewing for one of the most unhinged performances in cinema history. Davis chews scenery with such ferocity that she transforms psychological horror into high camp without losing the genuine terror.

movies.title: The Night is Short Walk on Girl

ratings.plot: In this comedy about one epic night in Kyoto, a college sophomore goes on a series of surreal encounters with the local nightlife, all the while unaware of the romantic longings of her classmate Senpai.

verdict.reason: Yuasa's direction transforms a single night into a kaleidoscopic fever dream that demands the big screen and full sensory immersion. Metrograph's DCP projection will let you feel the hand-drawn chaos at full intensity.

ratings.plot: Ordinary word processor Paul Hackett experiences the worst night of his life after he agrees to visit Marcy, a Soho resident that he met that evening at a coffee shop.

verdict.reason: Scorsese's funniest film is a masterclass in escalating chaos and one of cinema's great fever dreams about the city turning hostile. The newly restored DCP at Metrograph sharpens the neon-soaked Manhattan nightmare that defined 1980s downtown cool.

ratings.plot: Intent on seeing the Cahulawassee River before it's dammed and turned into a lake, outdoor fanatic Lewis Medlock takes his friends on a canoeing trip they'll never forget into the dangerous American back-country.

verdict.reason: One of the great survival films—see it on 35mm at Metrograph, where Boorman's control of landscape and danger plays at full force. The river itself becomes the antagonist, and the print restores details in light and shadow that streaming flattens.

ratings.plot: In the mid-19th century a mute woman is sent to New Zealand along with her young daughter and prized piano for an arranged marriage to a farmer, but is soon lusted after by a farm worker.

verdict.reason: One of the essential films of the 1990s demands to be seen on a theater screen, not streamed at home. Campion's control of image, sound, and performance—particularly Holly Hunter's wordless intensity—defines what cinema can do that no other medium can match.

ratings.plot: Two melancholic Hong Kong policemen fall in love: one with a mysterious female underworld figure, the other with a beautiful and ethereal waitress at a late-night restaurant he frequents.

verdict.reason: Wong Kar-wai's neon-soaked romance is essential cinema on the big screen. Metrograph's DCP presentation brings the saturated colors and kinetic editing to full life.

ratings.plot: A writer recounts a childhood journey with his friends to find the body of a missing boy.

verdict.reason: One of the best American films about friendship and growing up—see it on the big screen. Metrograph's DCP restoration brings out the golden-hour cinematography and the texture of small-town Oregon in a way that matters for this film.

ratings.plot: A professor in revolutionary Iran secretly gathers her most dedicated students to read forbidden classics of Western literature.

verdict.reason: Eran Riklis finds urgency in an act of quiet resistance that feels alive on screen. The intimacy of a clandestine reading group—where each book becomes an argument about freedom—demands the focused attention a theater gives you.

ratings.plot: Arriving in Chicago, Henry moves in with ex-con acquaintance Otis and starts schooling him in the ways of the serial killer.

verdict.reason: This is essential viewing on a big screen—a landmark film about violence that refuses to aestheticize or exploit what it shows. McNaughton's deadpan direction and grainy 16mm stock make the brutality feel documentary-real in a way that home viewing completely loses.

ratings.plot: A music group of girls need to learn to play a song before the school festival.

verdict.reason: A rare chance to see Yamashita's best film, a perfect balance of humor and heart about four teenage girls learning to play together. The DCP at Metrograph honors a restoration that brings out the film's warmth and the music's energy.

ratings.plot: Members of a street gang known as the Warriors must fight their way from the Bronx to their home turf on Coney Island when they are falsely accused of assassinating a respected gang leader.

verdict.reason: Walter Hill's stylized action masterpiece demands the big screen, and this DCP restoration at Metrograph is the place to see it. The neon-soaked NYC nocturne and the kinetic editing that defined action cinema belong in a theater, not at home.
A cult horror landmark that demands the big screen—Metrograph's DCP restoration lets you see Lon Chaney Jr. and the film's twisted family dynamics with clarity they've never had before.

ratings.plot: Legendary New York poet Ed Saxberger's forgotten works captivate an eccentric group of young creatives, reigniting his artistic passion. Their intrigue intertwines with the bewitching presence of actress Gloria.

verdict.reason: Kent Jones brings his gift for intimate character study to a film about artistic resurrection that earns its emotional stakes without sentimentality. The 90-minute runtime moves with the precision of poetry itself, and watching a forgotten artist find new life through unexpected connection is the kind of small, true thing cinema does best.

ratings.plot: A movie sound recordist accidentally records the evidence that proves that a car accident was actually murder and consequently finds himself in danger.

verdict.reason: De Palma's best thriller, a masterwork of paranoid cinema that demands the big screen for its elaborate setpieces and sound design. The climax alone—a meticulously constructed sequence at the Liberty Day parade—justifies the trip.

ratings.plot: Nicky is on the run from the mob, and he turns to old pal Mikey for help.

verdict.reason: Elaine May's only crime film is a masterwork of tension and betrayal that demands the big screen. The newly restored 35mm print captures the claustrophobic NYC nights and the fractured intimacy between two men in ways that streaming cannot replicate.

ratings.plot: When a southern Italian town is rocked by a string of child murders, the police and two urban outcasts search for the culprit amid scapegoating within the superstitious community.

verdict.reason: Fulci's masterwork uses genre machinery to eviscerate mob justice and provincial cruelty with unflinching force. The 35mm print at Alamo Drafthouse is the right way to see a film this visually precise about the anatomy of blame.

ratings.plot: A woman starts exhibiting increasingly disturbing behavior after asking her husband for a divorce. Suspicions of infidelity soon give way to something much more sinister.

verdict.reason: Zulawski's 1981 masterwork of marital breakdown and body horror demands the big screen—this is cinema as pure psychological torment. Metrograph's restoration unlocks the film's hallucinatory intensity and makes the creature effects register with their full, nauseating power.

ratings.plot: Several women enter a science fiction author's life over the course of a few years, after the author has lost the woman he considers his one true love.

verdict.reason: Wong Kar-Wai's most visually ambitious film demands a theater screen and Metrograph's DCP restoration lets the neon-soaked production design breathe. The 129-minute runtime tests patience, but the payoff is a rare work of sci-fi romance that uses visual style as narrative itself.

ratings.plot: A cab driver finds himself the hostage of an engaging contract killer as he makes his rounds from hit to hit during one night in Los Angeles.

verdict.reason: Mann's night-vision Los Angeles is a character unto itself, and the cat-and-mouse dialogue between Cruise and Foxx justifies the theatrical investment. Tom Cruise's silver-haired killer is one of cinema's most magnetic villains, and Mann shoots the city with the precision of a heist film.

ratings.plot: Green Beret veteran Rambo takes on a Pacific Northwest sheriff and the National Guard.

verdict.reason: This is a lean, tense thriller that works better than the sequels that buried its actual point about trauma and institutional cruelty. Sylvester Stallone's performance is genuinely affecting, and Ted Kotcheff keeps the action grounded in real geography and consequence for 93 minutes that don't waste a frame.

Klapisch's 1996 debut is a rare theatrical screening of a film that captures the texture of youth and sibling friction with genuine affection. The 35mm print at Metrograph restores the grainy, lived-in look that defines the film's intimacy.

ratings.plot: Two city-bred siblings are stranded in the Australian Outback, where they learn to survive with the aid of an Aboriginal boy on his "walkabout": a ritual separation from his tribe.

verdict.reason: Roeg's visual command of the Outback is unmatched on small screens, and this 35mm print at Metrograph restores the color and light that define the film's language. The cinematography is the story.

ratings.plot: Two pre-adolescent boys both experienced a strange event and later it affects their lives in different ways. One becomes a reckless, sexually adventurous prostitute, while the other retreats into a reclusive fantasy of alien abduc...

verdict.reason: Gregg Araki's unflinching direction and the restoration print justify the trip to see this film on a theater screen. The 105-minute runtime demands a committed viewing, and the restoration at IFC Center or Alamo Drafthouse reveals details that streaming cannot match.

ratings.plot: A bored New Jersey suburban housewife's fascination with a free-spirited woman she has read about in the personal columns leads to her being mistaken for the woman herself.

verdict.reason: Seidelman's best film—a sharp comedy about identity and reinvention that moves with real style and invention. Madonna and Rosanna Arquette create genuine chemistry, and the 1985 New York downtown energy gives the whole thing an urgency that holds up.

ratings.plot: A young martial artist is caught between respecting his pacifist father's wishes or stopping a group of disrespectful foreigners from stealing precious artifacts.

verdict.reason: Jackie Chan at peak physical comedy—this is essential 90s action cinema that rewards the big screen. The drunken style choreography is intricate enough to demand theatrical clarity, and Chan's willingness to wreck his body for a gag plays best when you can see every impact.

ratings.plot: A couple take a trip to Argentina but both men find their lives drifting apart in opposite directions.

verdict.reason: Wong Kar-Wai at his visual peak—worth the trip for a masterwork of color, movement, and heartbreak on the big screen. The DCP restoration at Metrograph lets you see every saturated frame and tracking shot as intended.

ratings.plot: New Orleans District Attorney Jim Garrison discovers there's more to the Kennedy assassination than the official story.

verdict.reason: Stone's maximalist conspiracy thriller demands the big screen, and this Metrograph DCP restoration brings back the visual assault that makes the three-hour runtime worthwhile. The editing, sound design, and cross-cutting between Warren Commission testimony and Garrison's investigation create a formal argument about how cinema can reshape belief.

ratings.plot: Two old pals reunite for a camping trip in Oregon's Cascade Mountains.

verdict.reason: Reichardt's most distilled film—76 minutes of genuine unease beneath stillness—plays differently on 35mm than anywhere else. The print at Metrograph restores the grain and color timing that makes the landscape feel as unsettled as the men walking through it.

ratings.plot: A step-by-step look at a murder investigation on the streets of New York.

verdict.reason: A procedural masterpiece that invented the template for every cop show that followed—see it on 35mm at Film Forum before it vanishes. Dassin shot the entire film on real New York streets in 1948, and the restoration lets you feel the pavement under your feet.

ratings.plot: A teenager just trying to make it through life in the suburbs is introduced by a classmate to a mysterious late-night TV show.

verdict.reason: Schoenbrun builds genuine dread from the collision between suburban dissociation and a show that bleeds into reality in ways that feel earned and strange. The 100-minute runtime keeps the uncanny tension taut without overstaying its welcome.

ratings.plot: The ethereally beautiful Vicky recalls her romances with Hao Hao and Jack in the neon-lit clubs of Taipei.

verdict.reason: Hou Hsiao-hsien's fluid camera and neon-soaked Taipei nights are essential on the big screen. The DCP restoration at Metrograph brings out the chromatic precision that defines this film's visual language.

ratings.plot: What did little Eve see--and how will it haunt her? Husband, father and womanizer, Louis Batiste, is the head of an affluent family, but it's the women who rule this gothic world of secrets, lies and mystic forces.

verdict.reason: A rare theatrical return for one of the finest films about family corruption and female perspective in American cinema. Lemmons' command of mood, color, and Southern Gothic atmosphere demands the scale and darkness of a theater screen.

ratings.plot: A day in the life of an unfaithful married couple and their steadily deteriorating relationship.

verdict.reason: One of Antonioni's essential works on marriage and modern alienation deserves a theatrical viewing. Metrograph's DCP restoration makes the glacial compositions and long takes hit harder than home viewing allows.

ratings.plot: In 1945, immediately following the end of Second World War, a woman who lives with her two photosensitive children on her darkened old family estate in the Channel Islands becomes convinced that the home is haunted.

verdict.reason: One of the best supernatural thrillers ever made, and Metrograph's DCP restoration gives you the chance to see Amenábar's shadows and silences the way they were designed. The twist lands harder on a big screen with an audience, and the craft—the blocking, the sound design, the slow tightening of dread—demands theatrical commitment.

ratings.plot: Two sloppy actors spend a weekend holiday at an uncle's country cottage.

verdict.reason: One of the funniest British comedies ever made—see it on the big screen where every line lands harder. Metrograph's DCP restoration sharpens the deadpan timing and gives the bleakness of 1980s London the visual weight it deserves.

ratings.plot: N/A

verdict.reason: A fresh adaptation that finds the darkness beneath Roald Dahl's premise without losing the magic, with a lead performance that nails both menace and charm. This is the kind of family film worth seeing together in a theater.

ratings.plot: Two roommates/physical therapists, one a vain woman and the other an awkward teenager, share an increasingly bizarre relationship.

verdict.reason: Altman's most cryptic and visually assured film demands the big screen—a dreamlike mystery that only deepens on repeat viewings. Metrograph's DCP restoration lets you see the pastel production design and spatial compositions that make the psychic entanglement between these women feel inevitable rather than explained.

ratings.plot: A reclusive retired professor is faced with confronting modernity when a group of vulgar youths led by an obnoxious marchesa take up residence in his unused upper residence.

verdict.reason: Visconti's final film is a sharp class collision that rewards the runtime with its glacial, merciless pacing. Metrograph's DCP restoration brings the palette of this Fascist-era meditation into sharp focus.

ratings.plot: A wealthy plantation owner is captivated by a mysterious woman with a shady past.

verdict.reason: Truffaut's best film about desire and deception demands the big screen, and Metrograph's 35mm print restores the saturated color and composed frames that make his romantic obsessions sing. The two-hour runtime clips along with real propulsion—this is pulp made by a master, not a slow study.

ratings.plot: After a car wreck on Mulholland Drive renders a woman amnesiac, she and a Hollywood-hopeful search for clues and answers across Los Angeles in a twisting venture beyond dreams and reality.

verdict.reason: Lynch's masterpiece is the rare film that demands the big screen, and Metrograph's 35mm print is the way to experience its impossible architecture of light and shadow. This is the night to see it.

ratings.plot: A disfigured composer sells his soul for the woman he loves so that she will perform his music, but an evil record tycoon betrays him and steals his music to open his rock palace, The Paradise.

verdict.reason: De Palma's 1974 fusion of Faust, The Phantom of the Opera, and rock opera is a formally dazzling cult film that rewards the big screen. The split-screen sequences, tracking shots, and operatic excess are built for theatrical immersion, not home viewing.

ratings.plot: During Prohibition, Treasury agent Eliot Ness sets out to stop ruthless Chicago gangster Al Capone, and assembles a small, incorruptible team to help him.

verdict.reason: De Palma's command of suspense and his ensemble cast—anchored by Connery's scene-stealing turn—make this a theatrical experience that hasn't dated. The ballroom shootout and Union Station massacre sequences demand a big screen and a crowd.

ratings.plot: In 1955 New Orleans, small-time private investigator Harry Angel is hired by a man who calls himself Louis Cypher to track down a singer named Johnny Favorite, but the investigation takes an unexpected and somber turn.

verdict.reason: A rare 35mm print of Parker's 1955 New Orleans descent into the demonic, where every shadow and reflection matters. The restoration and format make this noir-horror hybrid a full sensory experience.

ratings.plot: A disgraced ex-policeman who runs a small ring of prostitutes finds himself in a race against time when one of his women goes missing.

verdict.reason: Na Hong-jin's debut is a masterclass in tension and moral ambiguity that demands the big screen. Metrograph is showing it on 35mm, the only way to catch the film's savage energy and grimy Seoul cinematography in theaters.

ratings.plot: In the port city of Icheon, five female friends struggle to stay close while forging a life for themselves after high school. When one of the group, upwardly-mobile Hae-ju, moves to Seoul, the other girls deal with the loss in dif...

verdict.reason: A rare theatrical screening of a landmark Korean indie that defined a generation of female friendship films. Metrograph's DCP restoration sharpens the naturalistic performances and the film's attentive eye for how proximity to Seoul's money reshapes working-class bonds in ways that still feel urgent.

ratings.plot: Just after World War II, an American takes a railway job in Germany, but finds his position politically sensitive with various people trying to use him.

verdict.reason: Worth the trip for von Trier's audacious formal experiments and moral ambiguity in the postwar rubble. Metrograph's DCP restoration clarifies the dense layering of newsreel footage, graphics, and staged action that makes this film's visual argument about complicity and seduction unmissable on a big screen.

ratings.plot: On a dark, wet night a historic and regal Chinese cinema sees its final film. Together with a small handful of souls they bid "Goodbye, Dragon Inn".

verdict.reason: Tsai Ming-liang's elegiac final night in a movie palace is essential viewing on a theater's big screen. The DCP restoration at Metrograph honors both the filmmaker's precision and the cinema it mourns.

ratings.plot: Macbeth, the Thane of Glamis, receives a prophecy from a trio of witches that one day he will become King of Scotland. Consumed by ambition and spurred to action by his wife, Macbeth murders his king and takes the throne for himself.

verdict.reason: Kurzel strips the play down to blood and ambition, shooting it like a brutal medieval siege rather than a costume drama. The heavy use of smoke, shadow, and handheld camera work makes the violence feel immediate and the supernatural elements genuinely unsettling on a big screen.

ratings.plot: A swindler's activity indirectly caused a political crisis in France in the last years before World War II.

verdict.reason: Resnais at his most formally inventive, fracturing a financial scandal into shards of memory and style that refuse to cohere into easy narrative. The Metrograph DCP restoration makes the layered cinematography legible in ways the film demands.

ratings.plot: A middle-aged playboy becomes fascinated by the daughter of a private detective who has been hired to entrap him with the wife of a client.

verdict.reason: Wilder's most underrated romantic comedy deserves a theater seat, and this DCP restoration at Metrograph restores the film's visual wit after decades of dim prints. The direction is surgical—every shot places the camera exactly where it needs to be to catch a glance, a hesitation, a lie.

ratings.plot: A rough, short-tempered patriarch of a working-class family sees his life and the relationships around him slowly unravel.

verdict.reason: Gary Oldman's only directorial effort is a raw, unflinching look at working-class London that demands to be seen theatrically. The DCP restoration at Metrograph brings back the texture of his handheld cinematography and the brutal specificity of every domestic scene.

ratings.plot: International intrigue in London, involving an American university professor, an Arab prime minister, a ruthless businessman, a beautiful spy, and hieroglyphics.

verdict.reason: Stanley Donen's colorful spy romp deserves the big screen, and Metrograph's DCP restoration makes this the proper way to see it. The film's visual playfulness and breakneck plot earn their theatrical runtime.

ratings.plot: Fausta is suffering from a rare disease called the Milk of Sorrow, which is transmitted through the breast milk of pregnant women who were abused or raped during or soon after pregnancy. While living in constant fear and confusion...

verdict.reason: Claudia Llosa's formal invention—blending magical realism with Peru's trauma of political violence—demands the large screen and pristine image Metrograph provides. The 94-minute runtime respects the viewer while the visual density of each frame rewards full theatrical attention.

ratings.plot: A teenage skateboarder's life begins to fray after he is involved in the accidental death of a security guard.

verdict.reason: Van Sant's formal control over fragmented narrative and image—jumping timelines, Super 8 footage, elliptical editing—turns guilt into a visual experience rather than a moral lesson. Metrograph's DCP presentation locks in the deliberate haziness of the cinematography that makes the film work.

ratings.plot: Bouchra, a 35-year-old Moroccan coyote in New York documents her long-distance relationship with her mother in Casablanca, as they explore together the love, pain and secrets that unite them through calls and intimate conversations.

verdict.reason: A tender animated film about mother and daughter separated by an ocean, made with real affection for its characters and their fractured intimacy. The hand-drawn work captures the texture of long-distance love in ways live-action cannot, and Metrograph's presentation honors the filmmakers' visual specificity.

ratings.plot: Reminiscing about his dead son, a Vietnam War veteran attempts to uncover his past while suffering from a severe case of dissociation. To do so, he must decipher reality and life from his own dreams, delusions, and perceptions of ...

verdict.reason: Adrian Lyne builds genuine dread from ambiguity instead of jump scares, letting the camera linger on body horror and wrongness until you stop trusting what you're seeing. The 113 minutes feel earned because every hallucination is shot with the precision of something real.

ratings.plot: Aunt Mei's famous homemade dumplings provide amazing age-defying qualities popular with middle-aged women. But her latest customer - a fading actress - is determined to find out what the secret ingredient is.

verdict.reason: Fruit Chan's body horror masterpiece earns a theatrical visit at Metrograph, where its visceral images demand a dark room and loud sound. The 91-minute runtime respects your time while delivering maximum unease.

ratings.plot: A woman grows increasingly fascinated with her body after suffering a disfiguring accident.

verdict.reason: Marina de Van's debut is a fearless work of body horror that deserves the theatrical intensity of Metrograph's screen. The DCP presentation honors the film's unflinching close-ups and the precise craft of a filmmaker working through transgression and self-destruction.

ratings.plot: A love triangle develops between a vampire, her cellist companion, and a gerontologist.

verdict.reason: Tony Scott's feature debut is a visually sumptuous provocation that demands the theater—and this is a 35mm restoration at Metrograph, where the saturated color and precise compositions finally breathe. The film's baroque excess and formal control reward a big screen far more than any home viewing can offer.

ratings.plot: A violent police detective investigates a brutal murder that might involve a manipulative and seductive novelist.

verdict.reason: Verhoeven's pulp thriller holds up as a showcase of pure filmmaking craft and sexual provocation on 35mm. Metrograph's print restoration makes this the rare chance to see the director's control of image and rhythm exactly as intended.

ratings.plot: A newly-possessed high-school cheerleader turns into a succubus who specializes in killing her male classmates. Can her best friend put an end to the horror?

verdict.reason: Kusama's genre instincts have only sharpened since 2009, and this film's blend of teenage friendship and body horror feels prescient now. Metrograph's DCP restoration gives the neon-soaked cinematography the theatrical clarity it deserves.

ratings.plot: Set on the last day of camp, in the hot summer of 1981, a group of counselors try to complete their unfinished business before the day ends.

verdict.reason: This comedy has become a cult classic that rewards repeat viewing and plays brilliantly in a theater full of people who get the joke. David Wain's absurdist energy and the ensemble's commitment to deadpan nonsense make this a rare case where initial critical dismissal undersells what actually lands on screen.

ratings.plot: A Duke's son leads desert warriors against the galactic emperor and his father's evil nemesis to free their desert world from the emperor's rule.

verdict.reason: Lynch's version is a singular, visionary failure that rewards curiosity about how a master director approaches unfilmable source material. The grotesque production design and warped narrative logic make this essential viewing for anyone serious about science fiction cinema, regardless of its reputation.

Skip the new horror remakes and catch Nobuhiko Obayashi's 1977 masterpiece instead. Metrograph is showing it on 35mm, the only way to experience this hallucinogenic, formally wild film about a haunted house that operates on pure visual logic and dream logic rather than plot.

movies.title: The Bakery Girl of Monceau + Suzanne's Career

verdict.reason: Skip this if you need plot or spectacle, but watch it if you want to see Rohmer invent the language of modern cinema from a café table. These twin films are the foundation of everything that followed—shot on 16mm with the texture of memory, dialogue that feels like eavesdropping, and a camera that trusts you to find the meaning in a glance.

ratings.plot: Mongols with the help of an insider, ambush the influential Yang Family, defenders of the dynasty. The Mongols must hunt down all Yang survivors so their insidious plot to overthrow the dynasty will not be uncovered.

verdict.reason: Liu Chia-liang's martial arts masterpiece justifies the trip for its kinetic fight choreography and compositional rigor. The Metrograph screening restores a film that rewards big-screen viewing for its spatial clarity and balletic violence.

A newly struck print of Tsai Ming-liang's masterpiece deserves the big screen, and this is likely your only chance to see it projected as intended. The image restoration restores the film's glacial compositions and deadpan color palette to their full, agonizing power.

ratings.plot: A slow-burning epic chronicling the emotional journey of four thirty something women in the misty seaside city of Kobe.

verdict.reason: Worth the trip if you can commit to three hours of Hamaguchi's patient, attentive filmmaking about friendship and time. Metrograph's screening rewards the runtime with a proper theatrical space for a film that earns every minute of its duration.

ratings.plot: N/A

verdict.reason: A rare 35mm screening of a vital documentary about women's labor and dignity that deserves theater sound and image. Metrograph's print is the reason to go tonight instead of waiting for a smaller screen.

ratings.plot: In early twentieth century China, various criminals with different goals are connected to a Shanghai train, with many rich people on-board.

verdict.reason: Sammo Hung orchestrates a locomotive heist with the kinetic precision and humor that makes 1980s Hong Kong action cinema essential viewing. The train setting gives every stunt and fight sequence a built-in spatial logic that elevates the chaos above standard ensemble action.

ratings.plot: Members of a music band spending summer in the countryside watch the petty dramas play out among the local folks and among themselves.

verdict.reason: A rare Iosseliani restoration at Metrograph is the kind of programming event that justifies the trip. The director's gift for observational comedy and social texture rewards the 95 minutes on a theater screen where the light and sound matter.

ratings.plot: The story of a famous Brazilian criminal, called The Red Light Bandit because he always used a red flashlight to break in the houses during the night. Working alone, he also used to rape his female victims.

verdict.reason: A rare screening of a crucial Brazilian Cinema Novo film that redefined crime cinema through formal audacity. Sganzerla's debut is a restoration event at Metrograph, where a restored DCP of this formally radical 1968 work demands to be seen on a theater screen.

This is a rare chance to see a Broadway phenomenon on film, and it captures the theatrical magic that made the show essential live. The orchestrations and Rachel Zegler's voice carry an intimacy that only a camera can provide.

ratings.plot: Verdi's famous opera is brought to life in this production. The immortal tale of the noble Moor and his beautiful young wife, and of his lieutenant, whose jealousy and lust for power lead him to commit the ultimate treason.

verdict.reason: Zeffirelli's 1986 operatic adaptation demands the theater's sound system and scale—this is not a film to compress at home. Plácido Domingo's Otello and the lush orchestration of Verdi justify the subway ride and ticket price.

ratings.plot: Oscilloscope Laboratories presents CATVIDEOFEST 2026, a compilation of the latest and best cat videos culled from countless hours of unique submissions and sourced animations, music videos, and classic internet powerhouses. Each year, across the country, local theaters partner with nearby cat-focused charities, animal welfare associations, and shelters alike – a portion of ticket proceeds from every show goes directly to local cats in need.

verdict.reason: Seventy-five minutes of uncut cat content on a theater screen is the rare occasion when collective laughter beats solitary scrolling. Ticket proceeds go to local shelters, so you're funding rescue work while getting exactly what you came for.

movies.title: Butthole Surfers: The Hole Truth and Nothing Butt

ratings.plot: A documentary feature about the legendary American punk band Butthole Surfers. The film tells the story of how two accounting students from Trinity College in San Antonio found solidarity in their weirdness, recruited like-minded misfits – queers, weirdos, and nonconformists like naked performance artist/dancer Kathleen Lynch – and embarked on one of the most radical rock journeys of all time. Somehow this band, with a defiantly non-commercial name, ended up as a major influence on acts like Nirvana and even scored a No. 1 hit song. Beyond the band’s story, the film tells the human story of the people behind the band. It gives an intimate look at lead singer Gibby Haynes, guitar wizard Paul Leary, drummers Teresa Nervosa and King Coffey, and bassist Jeff Pinkus – five American originals with incredible personal stories.

verdict.reason: Essential viewing for anyone who cares about American punk's weirdest and most influential act. The film captures five originals at the center of a genuinely radical career, told with the kind of intimate access that matters for a band built on refusal to compromise.

movies.title: Grateful Dead Meet-Up at the Movies 2026

ratings.plot: Come celebrate the 35th anniversary of an iconic Grateful Dead show as it makes a high-energy return to the big screen! On August 8th & 10th, join Dead Heads in your neighborhood – and around the world – for the 2026 Grateful Dead Meet-Up at the Movies. This can't-miss event features the complete June 17, 1991, concert from Giants Stadium. The performance launches with a shocking "Eyes Of The World," finding the band in peak form from the very first notes. The setlist continues, seamlessly blending beloved classics like "Truckin'" and "Uncle John's Band" with rarities such as "Saint of Circumstance," "Might As Well," "New Speedway Boogie," and "China Doll." The major highlight of the night is the continuous teases of "Dark Star" edging its way in and out through the evening at six different points before finally exploding into the full song. The Dead capped off the spectacular night with The Band's "The Weight," a perfect song to send the crowd on its way. Considered one of the greatest shows of the band's final decade of performing, 6/17/91 offers a unique auditory experience as one of only two shows captured on 48-track tape. Enjoy a masterful surround sound mix by Jeffrey Norman and multi-camera visuals, featuring a rare cinematic appearance by both Bruce Hornsby and Vince Welnick. As a bonus, this extraordinary screening will also feature an exclusive sneak preview of the legendary "Shakedown Street" from the upcoming Merriweather 6/30/85 release, and a special introduction by Grateful Dead legacy manager and audio archivist David Lemieux. Join us, won't you?

verdict.reason: A once-a-year communal event screening one of the Dead's greatest shows in immersive surround sound on the big screen. The 48-track tape mastery and multi-camera presentation justify the theatrical experience, and the collective energy of Dead Heads in a theater on these specific dates cannot be replicated at home.

ratings.plot: Francis Ford Coppola's "A-side" to his gang war films and S.E. Hinton adaptations (with RUMBLE FISH being the "B-side") remains one of the defining films of an alternate-Brat Pack and '80s masculinity. Starring a veritable who’s who of ‘80s heroes and heartthrobs – Swayze! Cruise! Lowe! Estevez! – in some of the earliest roles of their careers. A teen gang in rural Oklahoma, the Greasers are perpetually at odds with rival group the Socs. When Greasers’ Ponyboy (C. Thomas Howell) and Johnny (Ralph Macchio) get into a brawl that ends in the accidental death of a Socs member, the boys go on the run. Soon, Ponyboy and Johnny, along with the intense Dallas (Matt Dillon) and their other Greaser buddies, must contend with the consequences of their violent lives.

verdict.reason: Coppola's definitive version of a formative '80s text deserves to be seen theatrically, especially with this cast at the peak of their early careers. The restored cut plays best on a big screen where the Oklahoma landscape and the precision of Coppola's framing actually matter.

ratings.plot: While investigating a plot to assassinate politicians, magazine photographer Friday Foster becomes a target herself.

verdict.reason: A rare 1970s blaxploitation action film with genuine craft and a female lead driving the narrative—see it on a big screen before it vanishes again. Arthur Marks shoots with real kinetic energy, and the 90-minute runtime respects the viewer's time while delivering the goods.

ratings.plot: From visionary director James Cameron, TERMINATOR 2: JUDGEMENT DAY is the ultimate sci-fi blockbuster that redefined action forever. Arnold Schwarzenegger is back. This time, he’s the protector. In a future ruled by machines, young John Connor holds the key to humanity’s survival. When a reprogrammed Terminator is sent back in time to protect him, a new threat emerges: the T-1000, a terrifying next-generation assassin capable of becoming anyone, anywhere. No rules. No limits. No mercy. As Sarah Connor races to stop Judgment Day before it begins, the fate of humanity hangs by a thread. Winner of multiple Academy Awards, T2 delivers iconic action, legendary one-liners, and groundbreaking visual effects that changed cinema forever. Back on the big screen this Judgment Day for the 35th anniversary.

verdict.reason: A landmark action film that still justifies the theatrical experience 35 years later. The T-1000's liquid-metal effects and Cameron's command of spectacle demand a big screen, and this anniversary run is the right time to catch it.

ratings.plot: Afro-Punk explores race identity within the punk scene. More than your everyday "Behind the Music" or typical "black history month" documentary, this film tackles hard questions, covering issues such as exile, loneliness, inter-ra...

verdict.reason: Skip the streamers and catch this 75-minute landmark doc on a theater screen where its urgent voice belongs. Spooner's 2003 film still cuts harder than most recent work on identity and belonging, and Nitehawk is the right room to sit with it.

ratings.plot: N/A

verdict.reason: Adult content with no theatrical distribution history or meaningful venue presence. IFC Center's programming suggests this is not a legitimate theatrical release.

ratings.plot: A traveling psychic who helps lost souls cross over encounters a powerful entity at a remote house. While investigating its origins, she uncovers dark secrets and faces a deadly threat from an unexpected source.

verdict.reason: A competent haunted-house setup squanders its premise on jump scares and predictable twists that feel like filler in a film that doesn't earn its runtime. The psychic-investigator angle collapses into standard possession tropes, and there's no visual or narrative reason to see this in a theater rather than at home.

ratings.plot: Woody, Buzz, Jessie and the rest of the gang's jobs are challenged when they're introduced to electronics, a new threat to playtime.

verdict.reason: Harris and Stanton deliver a competent sequel that feels obligatory rather than necessary, hitting familiar beats without finding new angles on these toys' lives. This is a home-viewing film if your kids are already asking for it.

ratings.plot: Follows the Minions in 1920s Hollywood as they search for frightening creatures for their monster movie, partner with a green creature, and must save the planet after unleashing monsters.

verdict.reason: Coffin's Minions spinoff is aggressively cheerful noise that exists to sell toys and serve YouTube clips, with no wit for adults and no substance for kids. Wait for the eventual streaming release.

movies.title: The SpongeBob Movie: Search for SquarePants

ratings.plot: Desperate to be a big guy, SpongeBob sets out to prove his bravery to Mr. Krabs by following the Flying Dutchman, a mysterious swashbuckling ghost pirate, to the deepest depths of the deep sea.

verdict.reason: Skip it; the theatrical cut offers nothing that justifies leaving home when the show is built for streaming audiences. At 88 minutes, this is a routine franchise installment with no visual spectacle or directorial spark that demands the big screen.

ratings.plot: In 1970s Detroit, John Miller falls for a local gangster's girl. In retaliation, the gangster enacts a frame job to send the innocent man to prison. Life ruined, Miller plots a revenge campaign against the man who took his girl away.

verdict.reason: Skip it; the premise is familiar revenge-plot material with a runtime that outstays its welcome at 103 minutes. There's nothing about Potsy Ponciroli's execution or the cast that makes this essential viewing on the big screen.

ratings.plot: A group of troubled teenagers are led by social workers on a California wilderness retreat, not knowing that the woods they are camping in have become infested by mutated, blood-sucking ticks.

verdict.reason: Skip it; the premise of mutant ticks attacking teens in the woods has aged into generic creature-feature territory with no theatrical urgency. At 85 minutes, it's short enough to stream on a slow night if the concept appeals to you.

ratings.plot: What seems to be the ideal setting for fun and relaxation quickly turns deadly when six vacationing college students encounter a cursed spirit with an insatiable appetite.

verdict.reason: Skip it; this is a forgettable slasher with no distinctive voice or visual style. The creature design and kills lack the ingenuity needed to justify a theatrical trip over streaming at home.

ratings.plot: Gru, Lucy, Margo, Edith, and Agnes welcome a new member to the family, Gru Jr., who is intent on tormenting his dad. Gru faces a new nemesis in Maxime Le Mal and his girlfriend Valentina, and the family is forced to go on the run.

verdict.reason: Skip it; the franchise has run out of ideas and this entry is just a 94-minute toy commercial. The theatrical experience adds nothing that wouldn't be better on a home screen in a few months.

ratings.plot: Los Angeles police officer Brian O'Conner must decide where his loyalty really lies when he becomes enamored with the street racing world he has been sent undercover to end it.

verdict.reason: Skip it; the theatrical cut is a clunky undercover procedural that hasn't aged well and the sequels have completely eclipsed the original. The Alamo screenings offer no restoration, format upgrade, or special event context that would justify the trip over streaming.

ratings.plot: Kara Zor-El, aka Supergirl, joins forces with an unlikely companion on an interstellar journey of vengeance and justice when an unexpected adversary strikes too close to home.

ratings.plot: Two-time GRAMMY®-nominated global girl group KATSEYE is coming to cinemas worldwide with a special theatrical release ahead of their third EP, WILD . Praised by outlets including The New York Times , Vogue , Rolling Stone , and Billboard , KATSEYE has earned acclaim for their relentless dedication to their craft and electrifying live performances. As one of pop's most exciting emerging global acts, the group continues to solidify its place as a worldwide force. From the same team that created Netflix’s POP STAR ACADEMY, KATSEYE: WILD HEARTS is produced by Interscope Films and Boardwalk Pictures, in partnership with HYBE X GEFFEN, and directed by Nadia Hallgren.

verdict.reason: This is a 80-minute promotional film masquerading as cinema, designed to sell an EP and deepen fan loyalty rather than stand as a theatrical work. Unless you are already invested in the group's fandom, you will get more out of the music and behind-the-scenes content on streaming platforms where it belongs.

verdict.reason: Will Gluck knows how to keep a rom-com moving, and Barbaro and Turner have the charm to carry a night-long meet-cute, but a gimmick premise about legalized hookups wears thin fast without real stakes. The setup is clever enough for a matinee, not worth rushing out tonight unless you trust Gluck's timing over the high-concept hook.

ratings.plot: Captured live over the course of GHOST’s two sold-out shows in Mexico City last year, 2 BIG TO RIG is the definitive document of the band's unforgettable SKELETOUR WORLD TOUR. verdict.reason: Skip the trip unless you're committed to the band; this is a live document for the faithful, not a gateway. The 16mm cinematography and phone-free setlist footage have real texture, but you're paying theatrical prices for what amounts to a premium bootleg.

movies.title: Michael Mann’s Manhunter: The Final Cut

ratings.plot: A retired criminal profiler (William Petersen) reluctantly returns to the FBI to help track down a serial killer of families and is forced to consult an expert – the imprisoned Dr. Hannibal Lecktor (Brian Cox in a subtly chilling performance). The third feature written and directed by Michael Mann is a gripping adaptation of the first of Thomas Harris' four novels featuring the iconic murderer Lecktor, and benefits from the filmmaker's typically striking visuals as well as a top-notch supporting cast, including Tom Noonan as the hunted killer and three-time Oscar nominee Joan Allen as his blind love interest. This new 4K final cut, overseen by Mann, enhances the film’s depth, visual clarity and sound, offering audiences the ultimate immersive version. Shot in 1985, MANHUNTER was on a frontier in both its subject matter and film form, initiating an impressive list of subsequent films and series. (Rialto)

ratings.plot: Winner of over 35 awards, experience the best of British musical HER-story in a live capture of the must-see musical sensation, SIX the Musical . The original West End cast reunite at London’s Vaudeville Theatre in front of a sold-out audience to strut their stuff and rewrite their Tudor traumas in an unmissable cinematic recording of the show packed full of style, sass, and sensational songs. Watched by audiences of over 3.5 million, SIX the Musical has become a global theatre phenomenon since its 2017 debut at Edinburgh Festival Fringe, where it has redefined the boundaries of musical theatre. The show tells the extraordinary story of the six wives of King Henry VIII, who step out of the shadow of their infamous husband and reclaim their own narratives.

verdict.reason: A filmed stage performance works best if you cannot see the real thing, but this West End capture on a theater screen lacks the liveness that makes musicals breathe in person. The 98-minute runtime respects your night better than a full stage show, yet you are watching actors perform for cameras in a playhouse, not for you in a cinema.

ratings.plot: Jigsaw is dead, long live Jigsaw. A direct continuation of the first four films in the SAW voyage, SAW V fully embraces the “gothic comic book soap opera” aesthetic to ask a simple question: How can the franchise continue after the death of serial killer Jigsaw and his faithful puppet Billy? The answer is more bizarre than you can imagine. SAW V is a stylized showcase for unbelievable practical gore effects, ridiculously complex traps, and baffling tangents that wouldn’t feel out of place on an episode of TWIN PEAKS: THE RETURN. Life is precious, watch more SAW movies. Screening an archival 35mm print courtesy of Lionsgate.

verdict.reason: Skip it unless you're deep in the franchise or want to see practical gore effects on 35mm film. The archival print at Alamo Drafthouse is the only reason to leave home for this one.
